::: {.lede}
I am a political and social data scientist and Assistant Professor in Public Policy at the [School of Government and International Affairs](https://www.durham.ac.uk/departments/academic/school-government-international-affairs/), Durham University. I study how governments design migration and asylum policy, what those policies do to the people they target, and how well democratic institutions represent the people they serve.
:::

My work on migration focuses on Latin America, especially Venezuelan displacement, and increasingly on Europe and the UK. I have documented that Latin America liberalised its asylum laws between 1990 and 2020 while OECD countries restricted theirs ([*IMR*, 2022](research/papers/liberal-region-asylum.qmd)). I have also shown that leftist governments adopted these laws largely as symbolic commitments ([*APSR*, 2023](research/papers/symbolic-refugee-protection.qmd)). My work on Venezuelan displacement shows that visa restrictions pushed many migrants onto irregular routes rather than stopping them ([*World Development*, 2024](research/papers/visa-restrictions-venezuela.qmd)). My work on democracy covers satisfaction with democracy, the representativeness of local councillors and political ambition among women.

I use quasi-experimental designs (difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity), survey and field experiments, original policy databases and computational text analysis.

I am a Visiting Fellow at the LSE Department of Government and an Affiliated Fellow of the IDRC Chair on Migration and Displacement at Universidad del Pacífico, Peru. Before Durham I was a Fellow in Political Science and Public Policy at the LSE School of Public Policy, and I completed my PhD in the LSE Department of Government. I have worked with UNHCR in Colombia, IFAD, UNODC, the Migrant Democracy Project and the3million.

**Media and policy enquiries:** omar.hammoud-gallego@durham.ac.uk. I give interviews in English, Spanish and Italian.
